title: Credibility assessment of explicit finite element models for cranial impact protection under ASME V&V 40
device: Cranial Impact Protection System (CIPS): a helmet insert comprising multi-density energy-absorbing foam and a low-friction slip interface

models.name: SBCE-FEM v2.1
models.what_it_computes: Coupled skull–brain explicit dynamics predicting skull linear/angular accelerations and element-wise maximum principal brain strain during impact

models.name: SSH-FEM v1.4
models.what_it_computes: Explicit shell–headform model computing center-of-mass linear/angular kinematics and contact force distributions with a simplified skull surrogate

mechanisms.name: Normal frontal drop
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Linear, near-normal impact dominates peak skull acceleration and focal brain response; aligned with certification-style drop conditions

mechanisms.name: Oblique lateral impact
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Tangential components elevate rotational kinematics that drive diffuse brain strain, a key injury pathway in real-world crashes

clear_factors: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU

deviation.detail: Credibility factor levels are reported on a 0–5 Credibility Attainment Index with 0.5-step granularity for each model–mechanism pair

sections: Computational models: SBCE-FEM v2.1 and SSH-FEM v1.4
Mechanisms of interest: Normal frontal drop and Oblique lateral impact

Context of Use (CoU): Pre-market evaluation of CIPS to predict skull peak linear/angular accelerations and 95th percentile brain strain in adult cyclists across normal and oblique drops; rationale—model outputs inform design iteration and pre-test risk screening prior to certification

Model Risk Level: medium–high; rationale—incorrect predictions could misguide design decisions with potential safety consequences, partly mitigated by mandatory downstream physical certification and post-market controls
Credibility plan and scoring approach (factor-by-factor, per model × mechanism) on a 0–5 index
Numerical code verification for explicit solvers (both models)
Discretization error estimation and mesh/time-step convergence (separate analyses by model and mechanism)
Model form justification and bounding assumptions (separate by model and mechanism)
Validation activities and their relevance to the CoU (protocols, kinematic/strain comparators, per mechanism)
Test samples: impact configurations, headforms, and material characterizations supporting validation
Software quality assurance: configuration control, defect tracking, and reproducibility evidence
Input parameters and equivalency considerations across test and simulation
Results: factor-level scores for each model–mechanism pair (matrix) on the 0–5 index
Discussion: interpretation of factor scores, dominant limitations, and implications for CoU decisions
Conclusions and next steps for regulatory submission
